match.reason: The bank card covers competition law (price fixing, misuse of market power, mergers) at Year 12 depth, but it does not teach the new point's core idea of price discrimination and multi-brand strategies to raise profit, so it is related rather than the same idea.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Card, fact: Product differentiation is defined as making a product seem different from rivals' products, but the example is one firm selling its own budget and premium brands. That sets a firm's own brands apart from each other, not from rivals, so the example does not match the definition. A student could also read a budget and a premium brand at different prices as price discrimination.
- Remember, wording: "But not by harming competition" suggests firms cannot raise profit that way. The card says such conduct is banned, not that it fails to raise profit. The line also drops the card's "generally" legal.

rejected.title: Business strategies to raise profit
card: Price discrimination
charging different groups different prices for the same good or service, such as cheaper tickets for students. It works when the firm can separate groups with different willingness to pay.
Product differentiation

making a product seem different from rivals' products through branding, quality, features or packaging, so buyers will pay more for it. One example is a firm selling a budget brand and a premium brand of the same item.
Anti-competitive conduct

acts that harm competition, such as competitors agreeing to fix prices. The Competition and Consumer Act 2010 bans these acts, and the ACCC (Australian Competition and Consumer Commission) can take action against firms that break it.
Price discrimination and product differentiation are generally legal ways to raise profit. Anti-competitive conduct is not.
rejected.remember: Firms can raise profit by pricing groups differently or making products stand out, but not by harming competition.

a.q: A cinema in Geelong charges students less than adults for the same film. Which strategy is this?
opts: Price discrimination
Product differentiation
Anti-competitive conduct
Price fixing with a rival
a.why: The same film is sold to different groups at different prices, which is price discrimination. It is not product differentiation, because the film is not made to seem different from a rival's film. Nothing here harms competition.
a.clue: Same product, different prices for different groups.

b.q: Two petrol stations in a Victorian town secretly agree to charge the same high price. What is true of this agreement?
opts: It is banned because it harms competition
It is legal because both sell the same product
It is legal because it is a form of price discrimination
It is banned because the price is above the cost
b.why: Competitors agreeing to fix prices is anti-competitive conduct, which the Competition and Consumer Act bans. It is not price discrimination, which means charging different groups different prices. A high price alone is not what makes it illegal.
b.clue: Look at who agreed on the price, not how high it is.

problems.detail: Product differentiation is defined only as 'selling several brands of one product'. In economics, and in VCE texts, it usually means making a product seem different from rivals' products through branding, quality, features or packaging. Running budget and premium brands is one example of it, not the definition, so students learn a narrow and misleading meaning. The chapter outline uses the same wording, so this may need fixing there too.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and have one clear right answer. The card defines product differentiation too narrowly, as only selling several brands, when it more generally means making a product appear different from rivals' products.

Multiple brands

selling several brands of one type of product, often at different quality levels, such as a budget brand and a premium brand. Each brand is built to appeal to a different group of buyers. They are different products, not one product sold at different prices.
Anti-competitive conduct

acts that harm competition, such as competitors agreeing to fix prices. The Competition and Consumer Act 2010 bans these acts, and the ACCC (Australian Competition and Consumer Commission) can take action against firms that break it.
Price discrimination and selling several brands are generally legal ways to raise profit. Anti-competitive conduct is banned, even though it may raise profit.
